```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(hypergraphs)
```

A document collection can be represented by a hypergraph of word
occurrences. In the document orientation, each document is a node and each
word is a hyperedge containing the documents in which it occurs. Incidence
weights record the frequency or term frequency–inverse document frequency
(tf-idf) of each word within each document. This representation provides
the input for structural summaries, document clustering, and label spreading.

This tutorial uses `covid_abstracts`, a bundled collection of 165
abstracts about COVID-19 and education published between 2020 and 2024.
The analysis constructs a weighted hypergraph, examines central words,
compares document partitions, and demonstrates classification from a small
set of labels. The examples distinguish descriptive results from evidence
about predictive performance.

## From corpus to hypergraph

First, tokenise the abstracts and define the vocabulary. The stop list
removes common function words and selected terms that are frequent in
research abstracts. `min_count = 3` retains a word only if its total count
across the corpus is at least three. These preprocessing choices affect
every subsequent measure and should be reported with the results.

```{r construct}
stops <- c(
  stop_words_en(),
  "using", "used", "use", "based", "results", "study", "research",
  "paper", "article", "findings", "data"
)

hg <- text_hypergraph(
  covid_abstracts,
  column = "abstract",
  id = "doc",
  weight = "tfidf",
  stop_words = stops,
  min_count = 3L
)
hg
```

```{r construct-values, include = FALSE}
edge_sizes <- hg_measures(hg, what = "edges")
corpus_summary <- hg_measures(hg, what = "summary")
participation <- subset(corpus_summary,
                        measure == "pairwise_participation")$value
```

The constructed hypergraph contains `r hg$n_nodes` document nodes and
`r format(nrow(edge_sizes), big.mark = ",")` word hyperedges. The median
word occurs in `r median(edge_sizes$size)` documents, and the most widely
distributed word occurs in `r max(edge_sizes$size)`. Tf-idf gives a smaller
inverse-document-frequency multiplier to widely distributed words than to
rare ones. Their final weights also depend on within-document counts.

```{r summary}
hg_measures(hg, what = "summary")
```

Pairwise participation is the proportion of document pairs sharing at
least one retained word. Its value is `r sprintf("%.3f", participation)`.
This summarises overlap but is not, by itself, a test of connectivity.
The clustering function checks that the document hypergraph is connected
before applying the spectral method.

## Central words

To rank words, reverse the orientation so that words become nodes and
abstracts become hyperedges. Clique-motif centrality then measures a word's
position in the binary co-occurrence projection. The score depends on
shared document memberships and the scores of neighbouring words; it does
not use the magnitudes of the tf-idf incidence weights.

```{r words}
word_hg <- text_hypergraph(
  covid_abstracts,
  column = "abstract",
  id = "doc",
  nodes = "word",
  weight = "tfidf",
  stop_words = stops,
  min_count = 3L
)
word_centrality <- hg_centrality(word_hg, type = "clique", sort_by = "clique",
                                 n = 10)
word_centrality
```

The first seven words in the centrality ranking are
`r paste(head(word_centrality$node, 7), collapse = ", ")`. Read these as
structurally central terms in the chosen vocabulary. A central term need
not be specific to a particular research theme.

## Clusters of abstracts

Set `type = "random_walk"` to use the Laplacian of the walk with
edge-dependent vertex weights (Hayashi et al. 2020). Here, the tf-idf
incidence weights determine the probabilities of selecting documents within
word hyperedges. The method embeds documents using Laplacian eigenvectors
and partitions the embedding by k-means. The example compares four clusters
with a coarser partition of three clusters.

```{r cluster}
clusters <- hg_cluster(hg, k = 4, type = "random_walk", seed = 1)
aggregate(node ~ cluster, data = clusters, FUN = length)
```

```{r cluster-years}
merged <- merge(clusters, covid_abstracts, by.x = "node", by.y = "doc")
cluster_years <- aggregate(year ~ cluster, data = merged, FUN = mean)
cluster_years
```

The mean publication year ranges from
`r sprintf("%.1f", min(cluster_years$year))` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(cluster_years$year))` across clusters. These means
provide a descriptive check of their temporal composition. Similar means
do not establish either thematic validity or the absence of temporal
differences within the clusters.

Cross-tabulate the four-cluster and three-cluster solutions to inspect
which document groups remain together when the requested resolution changes.

```{r sensitivity}
clusters_3 <- hg_cluster(hg, k = 3, type = "random_walk", seed = 1)
hg_agreement(clusters, clusters_3, what = "table")
```

```{r sensitivity-values, include = FALSE}
cross <- hg_agreement(clusters, clusters_3, what = "table")
kept <- function(label) max(subset(cross, label_x == label)$n)
size_of <- function(label) sum(subset(cross, label_x == label)$n)
```

The largest overlap with a single cluster in the three-cluster solution
contains `r kept("Cluster 1")` of the `r size_of("Cluster 1")` documents
in Cluster 1, and `r kept("Cluster 3")` of the `r size_of("Cluster 3")`
documents in Cluster 3. Cluster 4 contains `r size_of("Cluster 4")`
documents. The complete cross-tabulation shows how it is redistributed.
Cluster numbers are arbitrary labels and do not identify the same group
across separate fits.

## Classification from six labels

Label spreading propagates information from labelled documents through
the hypergraph (Zhou et al. 2006). For an illustrative task, label the first
three document identifiers from 2020 as `"early"` and the first three from
2024 as `"late"`. This deliberately small training set demonstrates the
interface; it is not a representative evaluation design for predicting
publication year.

```{r classify}
labels <- c(
  "2-s2.0-85085897904" = "early",
  "2-s2.0-85087124472" = "early",
  "2-s2.0-85087646998" = "early",
  "2-s2.0-85107489479" = "late",
  "2-s2.0-85112557152" = "late",
  "2-s2.0-85113355756" = "late"
)
predictions <- hg_classify(hg, labels = labels)
predicted_years <- merge(predictions, covid_abstracts,
                         by.x = "node", by.y = "doc")
aggregate(year ~ predicted, data = predicted_years, FUN = mean)
```

```{r classify-check}
hg_agreement(predictions, covid_abstracts, label = c("predicted", "year"),
             what = "table")
```

```{r classify-values, include = FALSE}
unlabelled <- subset(predicted_years, is.na(label))
unlabelled_early <- nrow(subset(unlabelled, predicted == "early"))
unlabelled_2020 <- nrow(subset(unlabelled, year == 2020))
```

Of the `r nrow(unlabelled)` unlabelled abstracts,
`r unlabelled_early` receive the label `"early"`; only
`r unlabelled_2020` were published in 2020. The predictions therefore do
not reproduce the year labels under this seed selection. Assessing year
prediction would require a defined target for intermediate years,
representative training labels, and evaluation on held-out documents.

## PageRank, the dual hypergraph and a null model

PageRank provides a document ranking from the damped walk with
edge-dependent vertex weights (Chitra and Raphael 2019). The ranking uses
both hyperedge selection and tf-idf incidence weights, so it cannot be
interpreted simply as the number of words or neighbours of a document.

```{r pagerank}
hg_pagerank(hg, sort_by = "pagerank", n = 3)
```

The `personalized` argument specifies the documents at which the walk
restarts. This produces a ranking relative to those restart preferences.
The dual hypergraph exchanges nodes and hyperedges by transposing the
incidence matrix, giving the word orientation without repeating tokenisation.

```{r dual}
dual_hypergraph(hg)
```

A null model assesses a statistic relative to a specified randomisation.
The swap model changes binary memberships while preserving each document's
hyperdegree and each word hyperedge's size (Gotelli 2000). The example uses
the abstracts published in 2020. It tests the structure of word occurrence,
rather than the numerical tf-idf weights.

```{r null-test}
abstracts_2020 <- text_hypergraph(
  subset(covid_abstracts, year == 2020),
  column = "abstract",
  id = "doc",
  weight = "tfidf",
  stop_words = stops,
  min_count = 3L
)
null_2020 <- hg_null_test(
  abstracts_2020,
  statistic = c("pairwise_participation", "avg_jaccard"),
  n = 99,
  seed = 1
)
null_2020
```

```{r null-values, include = FALSE}
pp <- subset(null_2020, statistic == "pairwise_participation")
aj <- subset(null_2020, statistic == "avg_jaccard")
```

Observed pairwise participation is `r sprintf("%.3f", pp$observed)`,
with a Monte Carlo p-value of `r pp$p_value` under the swap model.
Mean Jaccard overlap between word hyperedges has a standardised deviation
of `r sprintf("%.2f", aj$z)` and a p-value of `r aj$p_value`.
Interpret each statistic against its own null distribution. A result close
to the null does not prove random organisation, and an overlap departure
does not establish the substantive validity of the document clusters.

## Input from quanteda or tidytext

A long-format document–term table can be passed directly to
`group_hypergraph()`. Specify the document identifier, term identifier, and
count column explicitly. This permits the use of preprocessing pipelines
from quanteda or tidytext while retaining a clear definition of incidence
weights. The following code illustrates the required column structure.

```{r bridge, eval = FALSE}
# quanteda: tidytext::tidy() turns a dfm into a long table with columns
# document, term and count
group_hypergraph(
  tidytext::tidy(my_dfm),
  node = "term", hyperedge = "document", weight = "count"
)

# tidytext: word counts in long format (document, word, n)
group_hypergraph(
  my_word_counts,
  node = "word", hyperedge = "document", weight = "n"
)
```

## Choice of method

Choose the method according to the quantity of interest:

- `hg_cluster()` estimates a document partition. With
  `type = "random_walk"`, it uses the weighted incidence in the walk.
- `hg_classify()` propagates supplied labels. Its `margin` is the difference
  between the two largest class scores, not a calibrated probability of
  correctness.
- `hg_centrality()` describes structural position. Its interpretation
  depends on whether nodes represent words or documents and on the selected
  centrality definition.
- `hg_measures()` describes membership counts, sizes, and overlaps. Check
  connectivity separately when preparing a spectral analysis.

## References

Chitra, U., & Raphael, B. J. (2019). Random walks on hypergraphs with
edge-dependent vertex weights. *Proceedings of the 36th International
Conference on Machine Learning*, PMLR 97, 1172-1181.

Gotelli, N. J. (2000). Null model analysis of species co-occurrence
patterns. *Ecology*, 81(9), 2606-2621.

Hayashi, K., Aksoy, S. G., Park, C. H., & Park, H. (2020). Hypergraph random
walks, Laplacians, and clustering. *Proceedings of the 29th ACM
International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management*, 495-504.
<https://doi.org/10.1145/3340531.3412034>

Zhou, D., Huang, J., & Schölkopf, B. (2006). Learning with hypergraphs:
Clustering, classification, and embedding. *Advances in Neural Information
Processing Systems 19*.
